name: Magnitude Quantifier Construction

dimensions.function: Quantifies without precise count; emphasizes scale
dimensions.distribution: Heads quantificational NPs in subject, object, and other NP positions

1.definition: Plural magnitude noun quantifies an approximate large number

constraints.description: The core pattern uses plural magnitude nouns such as hundreds and thousands. Non-magnitude quantity nouns such as dozens have a related quantified use.
Distinct from partitive (two of the cats) where numerative is DP in fused-head function.
The of-complement NP may be indefinite (unlike true partitives).

projection.target: Hundreds of enquiries permits a bare plural complement. Exact two of the enquiries instead selects a subset from an established group. Plural hundreds of can give an approximate scale without fixing how many groups of a hundred there were.
projection.evidence: Reynolds distinguishes the plural magnitudes’ quantifier use from exact cardinal expressions and identifies dozen as outside the paper’s technical magnitude class.

curious.title: Hundreds of, thousands of, millions of
curious.summary: A plural word for a large size, followed by of, gives a rough, large amount without saying exactly how many.
curious.body: In hundreds of people, the word hundreds doesn't give an exact count. It gives a rough, large amount, and the speaker is emphasizing scale. The same pattern appears in millions of stars, and it can be stacked, as in tens of thousands of dollars. These are plural words followed by of and a noun phrase. Hundreds of people doesn't say how many groups of a hundred there were. That makes it different from an exact phrase such as two of the cats, which picks a smaller group out of a group already known. A related use with dozens is treated separately in this dictionary.
curious.try: Say hundreds of people and then two of the people. Which one tells you how many, and which picks some out of a known group?

teacher.summary: Helps explain hundreds of, thousands of and millions of as rough quantifiers, and why they differ from exact numbers.
teacher.explain: A plural magnitude noun (hundreds, thousands, millions) plus of and an NP quantifies an approximate large number. In hundreds of people, hundreds isn't a count of hundreds. It gives a rough scale without fixing how many groups of a hundred there were, and it can be nested (tens of thousands of dollars). The of-complement can be indefinite, unlike a true partitive such as two of the cats, which selects a subset from an established group. A word like dozens has a related quantified use but sits outside the core magnitude class. Mention that exact two of the enquiries is a different pattern.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an indefinite numeral, or a large-number noun. In this dictionary, a magnitude noun heads a quantifier construction, and a partitive is a separate pattern.

contrasts.note: Approximate scale; the complement can be a bare plural.
Exact, and selects a subset from an established group.

watch_for: A learner might read hundreds of people as exactly one hundred people, when it gives only an approximate scale.
A learner might treat hundreds of as a true partitive like two of the cats, when the of-complement can be indefinite.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of quantity phrases, some with hundreds, thousands or millions of and some with exact numbers. They sort them into rough and exact, then explain what each tells the reader.

child.hook: How do you say a really big number when you don't know the exact one?
child.explain: Words like hundreds, thousands and millions can tell you roughly how many. We say hundreds of people when we mean a big crowd. It doesn't tell us the exact number.

examples.text: We saw [hundreds of people] at the fair.

child.play: Look at the night sky or a big crowd. Make up sentences that start with hundreds of, thousands of or millions of, and add a noun. Which one would you pick for a huge number?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Magnitude Quantifier Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/magnitude-quantifier-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).
